name: Kala Lagaw Ya
confidence_why: Kennedy (1981, 1985) reports primary stress fixed on the first syllable with secondary stress on alternate syllables for the Saibai dialect, but Mitchell (2015) describes a contrastive system, with minimal pairs, in which most words stress the first syllable, a large minority the second, and certain affixes shift the accent, and since Kennedy himself wrote that more study of stress and morphology was needed, initial stress is the agreed default placement while the fixed-versus-lexical question leans to Mitchell.

catalog_quote: KENNEDY 1981:127-128: "The phonological word in KLY is defined by the potential pre-pause and post-pause and by the occurrence of word stress. Primary word stress is greater loudness, length and higher pitch on the first syllable. Secondary stress is of the same quality but less in degree than primary stress; it occurs on the remaining odd numbered syllables. Should an epenthetic syllable occurring second last in the word also happen to be an odd-numbered syllable, then the epenthetic syllable will not carry secondary stress. Rather the secondary stress will move to the final syllable. [gá.sam.a.dín] /gasamadin/ 'caught (dist. past)' *[gá.sam.á.din]" ... (8.2) "Phrase and clause stress occur on word initial syllables as does word stress." || KENNEDY 1985:99: "In KKY primary stress normally falls on the first syllable with alternate syllables thereafter bearing secondary stress." || MITCHELL 2015:362: "Contrastive word stress similar to the contrastive pitch accent of Meriam Mìr is present, though being lost in some (sub/idio) dialects. There are two types, inherent and shifted. Inherent stress is either on the first syllable (the majority) or the second (a large minority). Certain affixation can cause the accent to shift from the first to the second, or the second to the third, hence the term shifted stress" ... (p.363) "Sometimes, the pitch accent shift gives minimal contrasting pairs" púzika / puzíka.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: The phonological word in KLY is defined by the potential pre-pause and post-pause and by the occurrence of word stress. Primary word stress is greater loudness, length and higher pitch on the first syllable. Secondary stress is of the same quality but less in degree than primary stress; it occurs on the remaining odd numbered syllables. Should an epenthetic syllable occurring second last in the word also happen to be an odd-numbered syllable, then the epenthetic syllable will not carry secondary stress. Rather the secondary stress will move to the final syllable. [gá.sam.a.dín] /gasamadin/ 'caught (dist. past)' *[gá.sam.á.din] ... Phrase and clause stress occur on word initial syllables as does word stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of the phonological word; secondary stresses fall on subsequent odd-numbered syllables (3rd, 5th..), except that an epenthetic vowel in penultimate position is skipped and the secondary stress goes to the final syllable instead.
new_statements.secondary_stress: On the remaining odd-numbered syllables (alternating rhythm from the left); epenthetic penult skipped, secondary then on final syllable (gásamadín, not *gásamádin).
new_statements.exceptions: Kennedy: only the epenthetic-syllable adjustment; vowel length non-contrastive and co-occurring with stress (p.109); /a/ reduces to schwa in noun first syllables when the noun is phrase-unstressed (p.131). NOTE the later pan-dialectal sketch Mitchell 2015:362 (saved) disagrees in part: 'Contrastive word stress.. is present, though being lost in some (sub/idio) dialects.. Inherent stress is either on the first syllable (the majority) or the second (a large minority)', with affix-driven shifts (verbal noun -y, proprietive -lai; 3+-syllable verb stems shift to 2nd syllable in some finite forms, 'retained in full in Boeigu Kalaw Kawaw Ya and Kaiwalgau Ya') and minimal pairs like púzika vs puzíka.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (defined by potential pause and word stress); Kennedy adds that phrase and clause stress also land on word-initial syllables. Data are Saibai (Top Western / Kalaw Kawaw Ya) dialect.
new_statements.identity_note: Kennedy 1981 explicitly describes the Saibai ('Top Western': Saibai, Dauan, Boigu) dialect, i.e. Kalaw Kawaw Ya, Glottolog dialect kala1378 under kala1377. Mitchell 2015 covers all four dialects (Kalaw Lagaw Ya/Mabuyag mabu1248, Kalaw Kawaw Ya kala1378, Kaiwalgau Ya/Kaurareg kawr1234, Kulkalgau Ya kulk1234) and notes dialect differences in accent shift. Ray 1907's grammar is of the Mabuiag dialect.

sources.note: Sec. 8.1 (pp.127-128): primary word stress (loudness, length, higher pitch) on the first syllable; secondary stress on remaining odd-numbered syllables; an epenthetic penultimate syllable that would be odd-numbered does not take secondary stress, which moves to the final syllable ([gásamadín] 'caught'); phrase and clause stress also fall on word-initial syllables; vowel length non-contrastive and co-occurs with stress (2.3, p.109); /a/ -> schwa in first syllable of nouns in phrase-unstressed position (p.131).
